title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
author: Traditional Caribbean tale, retold — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Anansi the spider had a big pot. He said, "I will keep all the wisdom in the world in my pot!" He tied the pot to his belly and climbed a tall tree.

The pot was in front of him. It banged on the tree. Anansi could not climb well. His son watched from below.

"Papa," said his son, "tie the pot on your back! Then you can climb." Anansi felt silly. He was not the only one with wisdom after all. He let the wind take the pot, and wisdom spread to everyone.

questions.promptText: What did Anansi want to keep in his pot?

options.text: All the wisdom in the world

questions.explanation: Anansi says, "I will keep all the wisdom in the world in my pot!"

questions.promptText: How do you think Anansi felt when his son gave him the idea?
questions.explanation: The text says "Anansi felt silly" once his son solved the problem for him.

questions.promptText: In the story, what does "wisdom" mean?
questions.explanation: Wisdom means having good sense and knowledge — something Anansi wanted to keep for himself.

questions.promptText: Where did Anansi tie the pot?
questions.explanation: The text says "He tied the pot to his belly and climbed a tall tree."

questions.promptText: Who watched Anansi from below?
questions.explanation: The text says "His son watched from below."

questions.promptText: Why couldn't Anansi climb well?

options.text: The pot on his belly kept banging on the tree

questions.explanation: The pot "banged on the tree" while tied to the front of Anansi, getting in the way of his climbing.

questions.promptText: What word did Anansi call his son?
questions.explanation: In the story it is the son who calls Anansi "Papa" — Anansi is the father being spoken to.

questions.promptText: What does "climbed" mean in the story?

options.text: Went up something using hands and feet

questions.explanation: "Climbed" means Anansi used his hands and feet to go up the tall tree.

questions.promptText: Put these events in order: (1) His son gives him advice, (2) Anansi ties the pot to his belly, (3) Anansi lets the wind take the pot. Which happens second?

options.text: Anansi ties the pot to his belly
Anansi lets the wind take the pot

questions.explanation: Anansi ties the pot to his belly and climbs first; his son's advice and letting the pot go both come after that.

questions.promptText: What lesson does this story mainly teach?

options.text: No single person can hold all the wisdom in the world
Sons should not give their fathers advice
Pots should never be tied to trees

questions.explanation: Anansi tries to keep all wisdom for himself, fails, and it spreads to everyone — showing that wisdom cannot belong to just one person.

questions.promptText: Why does the story say Anansi "felt silly" rather than just "felt sad"?

options.text: Because his own child solved a problem he could not
Because he lost his pot in a storm
Because his friends laughed at his tree
Because he forgot the way home

questions.explanation: Feeling "silly" fits being outsmarted by his own son on something he thought made him special — not a general sadness.

title: A Trip to the Sea Wall
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
On Sunday, Maria and her family walked along the sea wall in Georgetown. The sea wall keeps the ocean water from flooding the city, because much of Guyana's coast is below sea level.

Maria saw fishermen casting their nets and children flying kites in the breeze. Her little brother bought a coconut water from a vendor. They watched the waves crash against the wall until the sun began to set over the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.promptText: What did Maria's brother buy from a vendor?
questions.explanation: The text says "Her little brother bought a coconut water from a vendor."

questions.promptText: Why does the sea wall matter for Georgetown?

options.text: It stops flooding because the coast is below sea level
It is a good place to swim
It is used to catch fish only

questions.explanation: The text explains the sea wall "keeps the ocean water from flooding the city, because much of Guyana's coast is below sea level."

questions.promptText: What does "vendor" mean in this passage?
questions.explanation: A vendor is a person who sells things — here, coconut water.

questions.promptText: What were the fishermen doing?
questions.explanation: The text says "Maria saw fishermen casting their nets."

questions.promptText: What were the children doing in the breeze?
questions.explanation: The text says "children flying kites in the breeze."

questions.promptText: How did the family most likely feel watching the sunset?
questions.explanation: A relaxed Sunday walk ending with watching waves and a sunset suggests a peaceful, enjoyable mood.

questions.promptText: What day did Maria and her family visit the sea wall?
questions.explanation: The passage begins "On Sunday, Maria and her family walked along the sea wall."

questions.promptText: What does "crash" mean in "the waves crash against the wall"?
questions.explanation: Waves "crashing" against a wall means hitting it forcefully and noisily.

questions.promptText: Which happened first: the family watching the sunset, or Maria's brother buying coconut water?

options.text: They happened at the same time
The passage does not mention either

questions.explanation: The coconut water is bought while walking, and the sunset is described afterwards, at the end of the visit.

questions.promptText: What does the passage suggest about why the sea wall was built, beyond just stopping floods?

options.text: It has also become a place where people relax and spend time together
It was built only for fishermen to use
It was built to sell coconut water
It stops children from flying kites

questions.explanation: Although its purpose is flood protection, the passage shows families walking, fishermen working, and children playing there — it has become a shared community space too.

questions.promptText: In this non-fiction passage, why might the writer have included the detail that "much of Guyana's coast is below sea level"?

options.text: To help the reader understand why the sea wall is so important
To describe what Maria's brother bought
To describe the colour of the sunset

questions.explanation: That fact gives the reason the sea wall exists at all, helping the reader understand its purpose before the family's visit is described.

title: The Kaieteur Falls
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Deep in the rainforest of Guyana lies one of the most powerful waterfalls in the world: Kaieteur Falls. Water from the Potaro River drops a single, thundering leap of over 220 metres — nearly five times the height of Niagara Falls.

According to legend, the falls are named after Kaie, a Patamona chief who paddled his canoe over the edge to save his people from an enemy attack, offering himself to the Great Spirit. Today, visitors travel by small plane deep into the interior to see the falls, and golden frogs live in the giant tank bromeliad plants that grow nearby, found nowhere else on Earth.

questions.promptText: Which river flows over Kaieteur Falls?
questions.explanation: The text states "Water from the Potaro River drops a single, thundering leap."

questions.promptText: What can you infer about Kaie from the legend?

options.text: He was brave and cared about his people
He was afraid of the water
He was a visitor from another country

questions.explanation: He "paddled his canoe over the edge to save his people", showing courage and care for others.

questions.promptText: What does "interior" mean in this passage?

options.text: The inland area away from the coast

questions.explanation: "Interior" here refers to Guyana's inland region, far from the coast, where the falls are located.

questions.promptText: How do most visitors travel to see Kaieteur Falls today?
questions.explanation: The text says "visitors travel by small plane deep into the interior to see the falls."

questions.promptText: Where do the golden frogs mentioned in the passage live?
questions.explanation: The text says golden frogs "live in the giant tank bromeliad plants that grow nearby."

questions.promptText: Why might the golden frogs be considered special?

options.text: They are found nowhere else on Earth
They are the largest frogs in the world

questions.explanation: The text states the plants they live in are "found nowhere else on Earth", making the frogs rare and special too.

questions.promptText: Who was Kaie, according to the legend?
questions.explanation: The text describes Kaie as "a Patamona chief who paddled his canoe over the edge to save his people."

questions.promptText: What does "thundering" describe about the waterfall's leap?
questions.explanation: "Thundering" describes a loud, powerful sound and force, like thunder — fitting for such a huge single drop of water.

questions.promptText: Using both facts in the passage, roughly how tall is Niagara Falls compared to Kaieteur Falls?
questions.explanation: The text says Kaieteur's drop is "nearly five times the height of Niagara Falls", so Niagara is roughly a fifth of Kaieteur's height.

questions.promptText: What does the passage suggest about how remote Kaieteur Falls is?

options.text: It is hard to reach, since visitors need a small plane to get there
It is easy to reach by a short walk from Georgetown
It is located right on the coast

questions.explanation: The need to "travel by small plane deep into the interior" shows the falls are in a remote, hard-to-reach part of the rainforest.

questions.promptText: Why might the writer have compared Kaieteur Falls to Niagara Falls?

options.text: To help readers understand its size using a waterfall they may already know
To say the two waterfalls look identical
To explain how frogs travel between the two
To describe the legend of Kaie

questions.explanation: Comparing to a well-known waterfall like Niagara gives readers an easy way to picture just how large Kaieteur Falls really is.

title: The Mashramani Costume
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Every February, Devika counted down the days until Mashramani, the festival that celebrates Guyana becoming a republic. This year, she had spent weeks helping her aunt sew a costume covered in sequins the colour of the Guyanese flag: green, gold, red, black and white.

On the morning of the parade, Devika's hands trembled as she fastened the last feather to her headdress. She had never marched before, and the thumping soca music from the speakers outside made her stomach flutter with nerves. When she finally stepped onto Republic Avenue, surrounded by dancers and steel pan bands, her nervousness melted away, replaced by a swelling pride that made her want to dance until sunset.

questions.explanation: The text opens: "Devika counted down the days until Mashramani."

questions.promptText: How did Devika's feelings change during the passage?
questions.explanation: Her "nervousness melted away, replaced by a swelling pride" once she began marching.

questions.promptText: What does "flutter" mean in "made her stomach flutter with nerves"?

options.text: To feel a fluttering, nervous sensation

questions.explanation: "Flutter" describes the fluttery, nervous feeling in her stomach before the parade.

questions.promptText: What colours were the sequins on Devika's costume?

options.text: Green, gold, red, black and white

questions.explanation: The text says the sequins were "the colour of the Guyanese flag: green, gold, red, black and white."

questions.promptText: What was Devika fastening on the morning of the parade?

options.text: The last feather on her headdress

questions.explanation: The text says "Devika's hands trembled as she fastened the last feather to her headdress."

questions.promptText: What can you infer about why Devika's hands trembled?

questions.explanation: The text says "She had never marched before" and describes her nerves — trembling hands reflect that anxiety.

options.text: The end of the rainy season

questions.explanation: The passage describes Mashramani as "the festival that celebrates Guyana becoming a republic."

questions.promptText: What does "swelling" mean in "a swelling pride"?
questions.explanation: "Swelling" pride means pride that keeps growing bigger and stronger as she marches.

questions.promptText: Put these in the order they happen: (1) Devika steps onto Republic Avenue, (2) Devika helps sew the costume, (3) Devika fastens the last feather. Which comes in the middle?

options.text: None of these happen in the passage

questions.explanation: The costume is sewn first ("weeks helping her aunt sew"), then the feather is fastened on the morning of the parade, then she steps onto the avenue.

questions.promptText: What evidence from the text best supports the idea that the parade atmosphere helped calm Devika's nerves?

options.text: She was "surrounded by dancers and steel pan bands" when her nervousness melted away
She spent weeks sewing her costume
Her hands trembled while fastening a feather

questions.explanation: The text directly links her nervousness melting away to the moment she is "surrounded by dancers and steel pan bands" on the avenue.

questions.promptText: Why does the writer describe the soca music as "thumping" rather than just "loud"?

options.text: It suggests a strong, rhythmic beat you can feel, adding to Devika's excitement and nerves
It means the music was too quiet to hear
It describes the colour of the music equipment
It shows the music had stopped

questions.explanation: "Thumping" suggests a strong, rhythmic beat rather than plain loudness, which fits the festival mood and Devika's fluttering nerves.

questions.promptText: What is the overall message of this passage about facing something new for the first time?

options.text: Nervousness before a new experience can turn into pride once you take part
Sewing costumes is more important than marching
Festivals should be avoided if you feel nervous
Only experienced marchers should join a parade

questions.explanation: Devika's arc — trembling hands and nerves beforehand, replaced by pride once she actually marches — carries the passage's underlying message about facing a first-time experience.

title: The Arapaima of the Rupununi
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
In the slow-moving rivers of Guyana's Rupununi savannah lives one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth: the arapaima. Fully grown, it can measure nearly three metres long and weigh as much as an adult human. Unlike most fish, the arapaima must surface every ten to twenty minutes to gulp air, since it breathes partly through a lung-like organ as well as its gills.

By the early 2000s, overfishing had pushed arapaima populations dangerously low in many rivers. Local Wapishana and Macushi communities, working with conservationists, established a community-managed fishery: fishing was banned in certain lakes, and villagers themselves monitored the population and guided the small number of tourists who came to see the fish. Within a decade, numbers had climbed back so strongly that the programme is now held up as a model of how local communities can protect the wildlife their livelihoods depend on.

questions.explanation: The text states it "must surface every ten to twenty minutes to gulp air."

options.text: Local people had a direct stake in protecting the fish
Fishing was allowed everywhere without limits

questions.explanation: Villagers monitored the population themselves and guided tourism, showing they had a direct interest in the fish's survival.

options.text: The means by which people earn a living
The animals living in a river

questions.explanation: "Livelihoods" refers to how the villagers make a living — connected here to fishing and tourism.

questions.promptText: How long can a fully grown arapaima measure?
questions.explanation: The text says it "can measure nearly three metres long."

questions.promptText: Which communities worked with conservationists to protect the arapaima?
questions.explanation: The text says "Local Wapishana and Macushi communities, working with conservationists, established a community-managed fishery."

questions.explanation: Since villagers guided tourists and monitored the population, protecting the arapaima became linked to their own livelihoods.

questions.promptText: What caused arapaima populations to fall dangerously low by the early 2000s?

options.text: A lack of air to breathe

questions.explanation: The text says "By the early 2000s, overfishing had pushed arapaima populations dangerously low in many rivers."

questions.promptText: What does "conservationists" mean in this passage?

options.text: People who work to protect wildlife and the environment
People who catch fish for a living

questions.explanation: Conservationists are people focused on protecting wildlife — here, working alongside villagers to save the arapaima.

questions.promptText: Using details from both paragraphs, roughly how long did it take for arapaima numbers to recover once the fishery programme began?

options.text: The passage says numbers never recovered

questions.explanation: The text says "Within a decade, numbers had climbed back so strongly" after the community-managed fishery was established.

questions.promptText: What does the passage imply about banning fishing in only "certain lakes", rather than everywhere?

options.text: It let some fishing continue while still protecting key breeding areas
It made no difference to arapaima numbers
It meant fishing was banned across the whole country
It was done to stop tourists from visiting at all

questions.explanation: Banning fishing only in "certain lakes" suggests a balanced approach — protecting some areas while still allowing the community to fish elsewhere.

questions.promptText: Why does the writer call the programme "a model" in the final sentence?

options.text: To show it as a good example other communities could copy
To describe a toy version of the fishery
To describe what the arapaima looks like

questions.explanation: Calling it "a model" means holding it up as a successful example worth following elsewhere, not describing a physical object.

questions.promptText: What is the writer's main purpose in this passage?

options.text: To show how community involvement can successfully protect wildlife
To warn readers never to visit the Rupununi
To argue that tourism should be banned everywhere

questions.explanation: The passage builds from the problem (overfishing) to the solution (a community-managed fishery) to the result (recovery held up as a model) — its purpose is to show community-led conservation working.

title: The Demerara Harbour Bridge Debate
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
For decades, the Demerara Harbour Bridge — a floating pontoon bridge spanning nearly two kilometres across the Demerara River — was the only road link between Georgetown and much of Guyana's west coast. Drivers grew used to the ritual of the retractors opening to let ships pass, sometimes leaving traffic queued for an hour or more.

When the government announced plans for a new, fixed high-span bridge, opinion was divided. Supporters argued that a modern bridge would finally end the delays and support growing trade and travel between the regions. Critics worried about the cost of such a large project and whether smaller communities along the route would benefit as much as the capital. Engineers, meanwhile, pointed out that the river's soft, silty bed made construction more complex than it might first appear, requiring deep foundations to support the structure's weight. Whatever its outcome, the debate reflected a wider question facing the nation: how to balance ambitious infrastructure with the everyday needs of the communities it is meant to serve.

questions.promptText: What kind of bridge was the original Demerara Harbour Bridge?
questions.explanation: The text describes it as "a floating pontoon bridge spanning nearly two kilometres."

questions.promptText: What is the writer's overall purpose in this passage?

options.text: To present both sides of a debate fairly
To argue strongly against building any new bridge
To describe only the engineering process

questions.explanation: The passage presents supporters' and critics' views, plus engineers' concerns, without favouring one side — a balanced, informative purpose.

questions.promptText: What does "infrastructure" mean as used in the final sentence?

options.text: Large-scale public structures like roads and bridges

questions.explanation: "Infrastructure" refers to large public structures and systems, such as bridges and roads, that support a community.

questions.promptText: What did critics worry about regarding the new bridge?

options.text: Its cost and whether smaller communities would benefit
That it would be built too quickly
That it would replace the harbour entirely
That it would only be used by tourists

questions.explanation: The text says "Critics worried about the cost of such a large project and whether smaller communities along the route would benefit as much as the capital."

questions.promptText: Why did engineers say construction would be more complex than expected?

options.text: The river's soft, silty bed required deep foundations
The old bridge had to be removed first

questions.explanation: The text says "the river's soft, silty bed made construction more complex than it might first appear, requiring deep foundations."

questions.promptText: What can you infer about the reliability of the original pontoon bridge?

options.text: It caused frequent, lengthy delays for drivers
It was used only by pedestrians
It had been replaced many years earlier

questions.explanation: The text describes traffic "queued for an hour or more" whenever the retractors opened, showing the old bridge was often unreliable for quick travel.

questions.promptText: What did supporters of the new bridge argue it would do?

options.text: End the delays and support growing trade and travel
Reduce the number of ships using the river
Remove the need for any road travel

questions.explanation: The text says "Supporters argued that a modern bridge would finally end the delays and support growing trade and travel between the regions."

questions.promptText: What does "ritual" mean in "the ritual of the retractors opening"?
questions.explanation: Calling it a "ritual" shows it was a regular, repeated routine drivers had grown used to, not a rare occurrence.

questions.promptText: Which two groups' concerns does the passage present as being in tension with each other?

options.text: Supporters wanting faster travel/trade, and critics worried about cost and fairness to smaller communities

questions.explanation: The passage sets supporters' focus on ending delays and boosting trade against critics' concerns over cost and whether smaller communities would benefit equally.

questions.promptText: What does the engineers' point about the riverbed add to the debate that the supporters' and critics' arguments do not?

options.text: A practical, technical challenge that could affect cost and time regardless of anyone's opinion
Proof that the new bridge should definitely not be built
Evidence that the old bridge should stay forever
A guarantee that the project will be cheap

questions.explanation: Unlike the opinions of supporters and critics, the engineers raise a factual, practical construction challenge that would affect the project no matter which side is right.

questions.promptText: How does the writer's word choice in the final sentence ("balance ambitious infrastructure with the everyday needs of the communities") affect the passage's tone?

options.text: It gives a thoughtful, even-handed tone rather than taking a side
It makes the passage sound angry at the government
It makes the passage sound like an advertisement for the bridge
It suggests the writer thinks the project is a waste of money

questions.explanation: Framing the issue as a "balance" between two reasonable needs keeps the tone measured and even-handed, matching the passage's overall fairness.

questions.promptText: The final sentence says the debate "reflected a wider question facing the nation." What is that wider question, based on the whole passage?

options.text: How to weigh the benefits of large infrastructure projects against their cost to ordinary communities
Whether ships should be allowed to use the river at all
Whether Georgetown should remain the capital city
How to design better pontoon bridges

questions.explanation: The whole passage builds toward this: supporters see benefits, critics see costs and fairness concerns, and engineers add practical complexity — together framing the broader national question of balancing ambition against everyday needs.
